newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees potential $100 mln jump in oil royalties.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees potential $100 mln jump in oil royalties.

text.p: A three-year battle between oil companies and the government will come to a head this year with the government proposing to change the way it calculates royalties owed by companies for oil they pump on federal land.

The proposed change, designed to capture the true market value of the oil, could force oil companies to pay an extra $100 million a year from 1998 or could result in no increase, said Minerals Management Service Director Cynthia Quarterman.
"We believe if companies were paying (royalties based) on pure market value, it shouldn't make a big difference to them," Quarterman said.
"If they were not, we should see a big increase in our royalties," she added.
The companies have said they have been paying royalties based on the real market value of their oil, which they peg to their "posted prices."
"Chevron firmly believes as we have stated in the past that our posted prices are a fair and accurate representation of crude oil in the field," a spokeswoman for Chevron Corp said.
But the Minerals Management Service, which annually collects about $4 billion in oil, gas and minerals royalties, said crude oil was usually sold at a premium to posted prices.

To cut out red tape in trying to read companies' books, the agency announced a proposal two weeks ago that would tie royalties to crude oil futures prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange and for Californian crude, tie royalties to Alaskan crude prices, adjusted for quality and location.
The $100 million estimate for potential new royalties was based on the difference between recent average posted prices and crude oil prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Rep. Carolyn Maloney, a New York Democrat, who has pressured the government to go after oil companies for delinquent royalty payments, praised the proposal.

"Using the current guidelines, the oil companies have easily buried the already understaffed ... audit teams in a maze of company trading transactions. The oil companies have also used legal roadblocks and endless appeals to prevent the relase of their affiliate's records," she said.
"Using the ANS (Alaskan oil) or NYMEX spot prices is by far the most efficient, accurate and least bureaucratic method to value royalty on," she said in a statement.

Quarterman said it was unclear how much resistance there would be to changing the royalty calculations, but noted that in comments on a proposal a year ago asking whether posted prices reflected market value, companies said either "Yes," or "no comment because we're in litigation about these matters."
Although it was announced two weeks ago, oil companies declined to comment on what impact it would have because details had not been officially published.
The agency plans to hold public hearings in the next two months in Denver, Houston and California on the proposal.
